question: A 63-old man is brought in by ambulance after a bar fight. Witnesses report that he is a bar regular and often drinks several shots of hard liquor throughout the night. The emergency department recognize him as a local homeless man with a long history of alcohol abuse. During the initial workup in the ED, he has a prolonged seizure and dies. An autopsy is performed that shows an enlarged heart with severe calcified atherosclerotic coronary arteries. Evaluation of his brain shows atrophic mammillary bodies with brown-tan discoloration. Which of the following tests would have most likely produced an abnormal result in vivo with respect to his nervous system findings on autopsy?
reasoning_chain: CHAIN: Chronic alcohol abuse -> thiamine deficiency -> Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome -> atrophic mammillary bodies with brown-tan discoloration on autopsy -> CSF IgG protein abnormal result in vivo -> 80%

CHAIN: Chronic alcohol abuse -> liver dysfunction -> decreased aldolase B activity -> abnormal result in vivo related to nervous system findings on autopsy -> Aldolase B activity abnormal result -> 70%
analysis: The autopsy findings of atrophic mammillary bodies with brown-tan discoloration suggest Wernicke-Korsakoff syndrome, which is commonly seen in individuals with chronic alcohol abuse. This syndrome is caused by thiamine (Vitamin B1) deficiency. Among the given options, the most likely abnormal result in vivo related to the nervous system findings on autopsy would be serum methylmalonic acid levels, as elevated levels are indicative of Vitamin B12 deficiency, which can also lead to neurological complications.
